title: Heredity
summary: Heredity is the passing down of characters from parents to offspring; it is controlled by genes. Variations are the differences between individuals of the same kind, even children of the same parents (free or attached ear lobes, tongue rolling, hitch-hiker's thumb, eye colour); they arise from different combinations of genes or from the environment. The science of heredity and variation is genetics.

Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884), an Austrian monk, worked for years with pea plants and was the first to state laws of inheritance, so he is called the father of genetics; his work was recognised only after Correns, Tschermak and de Vries reached the same results. (1) Law of segregation: every character (flower colour, plant height, seed colour and texture, pod colour and shape, flower position) is controlled by a pair of factors, which separate during gamete formation so that each gamete gets one; on fertilisation the pair is restored. (2) Law of dominance: of the two factors, the dominant one expresses itself even when the other is present; the recessive one expresses only when the dominant is absent — tallness is dominant over dwarfness in pea. He also proposed the laws of independent assortment and parental equivalence. In 1902 Sutton showed that Mendel's factors lie on chromosomes; they are now called genes.

Chromosomes are in the nucleus of every cell (except mammalian red blood cells). They occur in pairs, one from the father and one from the mother; they are seen only during cell division (otherwise they form a network called chromatin); their number is fixed for each species (diploid number, 2n); each is made of one DNA molecule and proteins. Before cell division the DNA replicates so each chromosome has two chromatids joined at the centromere, which separate into the two daughter cells. Bacteria have a single circular chromosome lying in the cytoplasm (nucleoid).

Human body cells have 46 chromosomes (2n = 46); gametes have 23 (haploid). Of the 23 pairs, 22 pairs are autosomes and the 23rd pair are the sex chromosomes — XX in females and XY in males. The Y chromosome carries genes for maleness (testis-determining factor).

Genes, the units of heredity, are segments of the DNA of a chromosome and occur in pairs at the same place on homologous chromosomes. DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polynucleotide; each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a deoxyribose sugar and a phosphate. There are four bases — adenine, guanine, thymine and cytosine — hence four kinds of nucleotides. DNA is a double helix of two strands. Since every cell of a person has identical DNA, unique to that person and resembling the parents', DNA fingerprinting from hair, blood or semen can identify criminals or settle parentage. Dr Hargobind Khorana made the first artificial gene (Nobel Prize, 1968).

DNA replication (before cell division): (1) enzymes unwind the double helix, exposing the two strands; (2) DNA polymerase builds a new daughter strand on each parent strand, giving two DNA molecules, each with one old and one new strand; (3) the two identical molecules become the two chromatids joined by the centromere, which separate during cell division.

Human blood groups A, B, AB and O are controlled by three genes, Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i; each person has two, one from each parent. IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi → A; IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi → B; IᴬIᴮ → AB; ii → O. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are dominant and i is recessive. Rh+ is dominant over Rh−. O is the universal donor and AB the universal recipient; for an accident victim of unknown group the safest blood is O negative (ii, Rh−).

Eggs are of one kind (22 + X). Sperms are of two kinds (22 + X or 22 + Y). An X-bearing sperm fusing with the egg gives a girl (44 + XX); a Y-bearing sperm gives a boy (44 + XY). The sex of a child is therefore decided by the father's sperm and purely by chance, so blaming a woman for not bearing a son is wrong. The Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques Act (1994, in force from 1996) bans finding and disclosing the sex of a foetus, to check female foeticide.

A genetic disorder results when a defective (mutated) gene is inherited — a dominant one, or a recessive one from both parents; medicines cannot cure it, but gene replacement therapy is being developed. Thalassemia (autosomal): the person cannot make haemoglobin for red blood cells and needs frequent transfusions. Haemophilia: blood does not clot because the clotting substance is missing. Colour-blindness: usually inability to tell blue from green. The genes for haemophilia and colour-blindness are on the X chromosome, so they are passed from a carrier mother to her son; a son has only one X, so the defect is not masked, while a daughter's second X usually carries a normal gene. Consanguineous marriages (between close relatives) raise the chance that both parents carry the same defective recessive gene; genetic counsellors tell couples the chances of such disorders so they can make informed decisions.

The genome is the full set of genes of an organism; the human genome was mapped in 2003, helping to find therapies for genetic defects. Genetic engineering (recombinant DNA technique) transfers a gene from one species into another, producing a genetically modified organism (GMO). The DNA is cut with restriction enzymes and the gene is carried by plasmids (small circular DNA in bacteria, separate from the chromosome) or by bacteriophages; a bacterial clone then multiplies the gene, e.g. to make human insulin or for gene therapy.

vsa: Name two plant characteristics that are controlled by a pair of Mendel's factors.
Any two: height of the plant (tall/dwarf), colour of the flower, colour or texture of the seed, colour or shape of the pod, position of the flower.
Name the four kinds of nucleotides in DNA.
Nucleotides with the bases adenine (A), guanine (G), thymine (T) and cytosine (C).
What are autosomes? How many pairs of autosomes are there in a human cell?
Autosomes are the chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes; they carry genes for body characters. A human cell has 22 pairs.

or: State the two laws of heredity given by Mendel.

(1) Law of segregation: each character is controlled by a pair of factors that separate during gamete formation, one going to each gamete. (2) Law of dominance: of a pair of factors one (dominant) expresses itself even in the presence of the other (recessive).

vsa: Why is genetic counselling advisable before marriage between close relatives?

Close relatives may carry the same defective recessive gene; their children are more likely to get two copies and suffer from a genetic disorder. Counselling tells the couple the chances so they can decide wisely.
What is DNA fingerprinting? Give one use.
Identifying a person from the unique pattern of their DNA. It is used to identify criminals from hair or blood left at a crime scene, or to settle disputed parentage.
A genetically modified organism — one into whose genome a gene from another species has been inserted by genetic engineering.
sa: Explain the chromosomal basis of sex determination in humans with a line diagram.

Father 44 + XY produces two kinds of sperms (22 + X and 22 + Y); mother 44 + XX produces one kind of egg (22 + X). Egg (22 + X) + sperm (22 + X) → 44 + XX (girl); egg (22 + X) + sperm (22 + Y) → 44 + XY (boy). The chance of each is 50%, and the sex is decided by the sperm.
Name three genetic disorders. On which chromosome are the genes of colour-blindness and haemophilia found, and why are these disorders more common in boys?

Thalassemia, haemophilia, colour-blindness. The genes are on the X chromosome. A boy has only one X (from his mother) and a Y; if that X carries the defective gene there is no normal gene to mask it, so he shows the disorder. A girl has two X chromosomes, and the normal gene on one usually masks the defective one.
What are genes and what is their chemical nature? What genes will a child with blood group O have?

Genes are the units of heredity, located at fixed points on chromosomes; chemically they are segments of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). A child with blood group O has the genes ii (one recessive i from each parent).
State two characteristics of chromosomes. Write the three main steps of DNA replication.

Chromosomes occur in pairs (one from each parent) and in a fixed number for each species; each is made of one DNA molecule and proteins. Replication: (1) the double helix unwinds with the help of enzymes; (2) DNA polymerase builds a new strand on each old strand, giving two DNA molecules; (3) the two identical molecules form two chromatids joined at the centromere.
What is meant by the law of dominance? Explain with an example.

When two contrasting factors are present, only one (dominant) expresses itself; the other (recessive) shows only when the dominant one is absent. In pea, a plant with one factor for tallness and one for dwarfness is tall; dwarfness shows only when both factors are for dwarfness.
la: Describe the process of DNA replication. Name the four bases found in DNA.

Before a cell divides, each DNA molecule makes a copy of itself. (1) Enzymes unwind the double helix and separate the two strands. (2) The enzyme DNA polymerase builds a new complementary strand on each parental strand, so two DNA molecules form, each with one old and one new strand (semi-conservative). (3) The two identical DNA molecules become two chromatids joined at the centromere; during cell division they separate, one going to each daughter cell. Bases: adenine, guanine, thymine and cytosine.

la.note: October 2017 also asked why chromatids form before cell division — so that each daughter cell receives an identical copy of every chromosome.

la: Explain the inheritance of ABO blood groups in humans. Why is O called the universal donor and AB the universal recipient?

Blood groups are controlled by three genes — Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i — of which each person carries two, one from each parent. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are dominant over i and are equal to each other. IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi give group A; IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi give group B; IᴬIᴮ gives AB; ii gives O. A child of an Iᴬi father and an Iᴮi mother can have A, B, AB or O. O blood can be given to people of all four groups, so O is the universal donor; AB people can receive blood of any group, so AB is the universal recipient. The safest blood in an emergency is O negative.
What are hereditary disorders? Describe thalassemia, haemophilia and colour-blindness and explain the role of genetic counselling.

A hereditary disorder is caused by a defective gene passed from parents to offspring; it cannot be cured by medicines. Thalassemia: an autosomal disorder in which the person cannot make haemoglobin and needs frequent blood transfusions. Haemophilia: the clotting substance is missing, so bleeding does not stop. Colour-blindness: inability to distinguish colours such as blue and green. Haemophilia and colour-blindness genes are on the X chromosome and pass from carrier mothers to sons. Genetic counselling tells couples, especially close relatives, the probability of a disorder in their children so that they can make informed decisions.
What is genetic engineering? Outline its main steps and give two benefits.

Genetic engineering (recombinant DNA technique) transfers a gene from one organism into another species. Steps: the required gene is cut from the donor DNA with a restriction enzyme; a plasmid is cut open with the same enzyme; the gene is joined into the plasmid, forming recombinant DNA; the plasmid is put into a bacterium, which multiplies into a clone that carries and expresses the gene. Benefits: production of human insulin and vaccines; gene therapy for genetic disorders; crops with pest resistance or better nutrition (GM crops).
